content.narrative_summary: Section 1.4 outlines the purpose of the ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline, superseding prior device‐based therapy recommendations and targeting adult patients (>18 years) with bradycardia or conduction disorders. It lists specific objectives including clinical significance, diagnostic evaluation, and treatment modalities. Section 1.5 defines the Class of Recommendation (COR) and Level of Evidence (LOE) frameworks used in the guideline. Section 1.6 provides a table of abbreviations and their defined meanings used throughout the document.

content.narrative_summary: Slower heart rates and changes in intercellular conduction can occur as part of normal aging and disease progression, leading to bradycardia and conduction abnormalities often seen in the elderly. Abnormalities of the sinus node, atrial tissue, atrioventricular nodal tissue, and specialized conduction system contribute to discordant atrial and ventricular depolarization and abnormal ventricular depolarization. Sinus node dysfunction (SND) is described as age-dependent degenerative fibrosis of sinus nodal tissue and surrounding atrial myocardium, resulting in abnormal impulse formation and propagation.

content.narrative_summary: Degenerative fibrosis underlies various bradycardia and pause‐related syndromes and can coexist with atrial arrhythmias (‘tachy‐brady syndrome’). Heart block occurs in some patients who have required permanent atrial pacing for sinus node dysfunction (SND), suggesting fibrotic involvement of the atrioventricular conduction system. Data from permanent pacemaker studies and large ARIC and CHS cohorts show that SND is most common in patients in their 70s or 80s and parallels rates of pacemaker implantation for atrioventricular nodal disease. In these patients, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, valvular heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, and atrial fibrillation are frequent comorbidities. Intrinsic sinus and atrioventricular nodal diseases present similarly.

section_headings: 4.2.1 Resting ECG in Patients With Documented or Suspected Bradycardia or Conduction Disorders
4.2.2 Exercise Electrocardiographic Testing in Patients With Documented or Suspected Bradycardia or Conduction Disorders
content.narrative_summary: The resting ECG is an essential component of the initial evaluation for known or suspected bradycardia or conduction disorders. A timely 12-lead ECG can provide a definitive diagnosis, document rhythm, rate, conduction disturbances, and detect structural or systemic disease. While diagnostic yield is low (<5%) in nonspecific presentations, an abnormal initial ECG predicts adverse outcomes in syncope. Exercise ECG testing has no routine role but may be reasonable in patients with suspected chronotropic incompetence or exercise-related symptoms to aid diagnosis and prognosis.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with suspected bradycardia or conduction disorder, a 12-lead ECG is recommended to document rhythm, rate, and conduction, and to screen for structural heart disease or systemic illness (S4.2.1–S4.2.1–4).

content.title: 4.2.4. Imaging in Patients With Documented or Suspected Bradycardia or Conduction Disorders
section_headings: 4.2.4. Imaging in Patients With Documented or Suspected Bradycardia or Conduction Disorders
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis emphasizes that bradycardia and conduction disorders often coexist with structural heart disease and that assessment of cardiac structure via echocardiography is frequently performed in these patients. Surveys indicate high rates of echocardiographic use (66% always/almost always, 27% often). Advanced imaging modalities can be helpful in selected cases when structural disease is suspected. Supportive text notes that patients with left bundle branch block (LBBB) have increased prevalence of cardiovascular comorbidities and structural disease, with associated risks of death and heart failure, even without increased all-cause mortality. Excluding structural heart disease in LBBB is prudent due to its prognostic implications.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Cardiac Imaging in Bradycardia or Conduction Disorders

rows.recommendation: In patients with newly identified LBBB, second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block, high-grade atrioventricular block, or third-degree atrioventricular block with or without apparent structural heart disease or coronary artery disease, transthoracic echocardiography is recommended (S4.2.4-1–S4.2.4-10).

In selected patients presenting with bradycardia or conduction disorders other than LBBB, second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block, high-grade atrioventricular block, or third-degree atrioventricular block, transthoracic echocardiography is reasonable if structural heart disease is suspected (S4.2.4-3, S4.2.4-11–S4.2.4-13).

In selected patients with bradycardia or bundle branch block, disease-specific advanced imaging (e.g., transesophageal echocardiography, computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], or nuclear imaging) is reasonable if structural heart disease is suspected yet not confirmed by other diagnostic modalities (S4.2.4-14–S4.2.4-22).

In the evaluation of patients with asymptomatic sinus bradycardia or first-degree atrioventricular block and no clinical evidence of structural heart disease, routine cardiac imaging is not indicated (S4.2.4-22–S4.2.4-24).

section_headings: 4.2.7. Sleep Apnea Evaluation and Treatment in Patients With Documented or Suspected Bradycardia or Conduction Disorders
content.narrative_summary: The page opens mid-discussion of genetic testing in sinus node dysfunction (SND) and conduction disease, noting that most SND is physiologic or acquired, genetic testing is not routinely indicated due to undefined diagnostic yield and uncertain variant significance, and the writing committee does not endorse routine testing except in select cases. Section 4.2.7 then provides a synopsis explaining that nocturnal bradyarrhythmias (sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, blocks, junctional rhythm, asystole) are common but often asymptomatic, decline with age, and are less frequent with CPAP in sleep apnea patients who are unlikely to develop symptomatic bradycardia long-term; treating sleep apnea not only alleviates apnea-related symptoms and improves cardiovascular outcomes but can often eliminate the need for pacemaker implantation. The beginning of Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text (point 1) describes the prevalence of sleep-disordered breathing in the US (24% men, 9% women; higher in cardiovascular disease populations) and rates of profound nocturnal sinus bradycardia and AV block ranges, ending with a description of a stereotypical apneic bradycardia pattern cited as an ECG diagnostic cue.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Sleep Apnea Evaluation and Treatment in Patients With Documented or Suspected Bradycardia or Conduction Disorders

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with documented or suspected bradycardia or conduction disorder during sleep, screening for symptoms of sleep apnea syndrome is recommended with subsequent confirmatory testing directed by clinical suspicion (S4.2.7-1–S4.2.7-11).

2. In patients with sleep-related bradycardia or conduction disorder and documented obstructive sleep apnea, treatment directed specifically at the sleep apnea (e.g., continuous positive airway pressure and weight loss) is recommended (S4.2.7-12–S4.2.7-16).
3. In patients who have previously received or are being considered for a PPM for bradycardia or conduction disorder, screening for sleep apnea syndrome is reasonable (S4.2.7-10, S4.2.7-11).

content.narrative_summary: The methylxanthines theophylline and aminophylline exert positive chronotropic effects on the heart, likely via adenosine antagonism at the sinoatrial node. section_headings: 5.3.3. Temporary Pacing for Bradycardia Attributable to SND
content.narrative_summary: Temporary pacing, which usually can be withdrawn after 4 to 6 weeks with rare side effects or adverse events, is used to acutely treat hemodynamically significant sinus bradycardia attributable to sinus node dysfunction (SND). It addresses prolonged symptomatic pauses, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, or reversible causes of severe bradycardia with the goal of avoiding permanent pacemaker implantation. Modalities include transcutaneous, transesophageal, transvenous pacing electrodes, and pulmonary-arterial pacing catheters, generally pacing the right ventricle for ease of access; in select cases atrial pacing (alone or with ventricular pacing) is used to maintain atrioventricular synchrony.

rows.recommendation: In patients with persistent hemodynamically unstable SND refractory to medical therapy, temporary transvenous pacing is reasonable to increase heart rate and improve symptoms until a PPM is placed or the bradycardia resolves (5.3.3-3—5.3.3-17).

In patients with SND with severe symptoms or hemodynamic compromise, temporary transcutaneous pacing may be considered to increase heart rate and improve symptoms until a temporary transvenous or PPM is placed or the bradycardia resolves (5.3.3-1, 5.3.3-18—5.3.3-22).

In patients with SND with minimal and/or infrequent symptoms without hemodynamic compromise, temporary transcutaneous or transvenous pacing should not be performed (5.3.3-4, 5.3.3-6, 5.3.3-7, 5.3.3-12, 5.3.3-14—5.3.3-16, 5.3.3-23).

5.4.1. General Principles of Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to SND
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis states that anti-bradycardia therapy in sinus node dysfunction (SND) aims to increase heart rate and maintain organ perfusion. There is no defined minimum heart rate for treatment, emphasizing the need to correlate symptoms with bradycardia and to identify reversible extrinsic causes (metabolic, endocrine, infection, medications). Permanent pacing may be required for intrinsic SND but carries procedural risks, including complications from implantation and long-term lead management. High parasympathetic tone during rest or sleep often causes benign sinus bradycardia or pauses, which usually do not require pacing.

In patients with asymptomatic SND, or in those in whom the symptoms have been documented to occur in the absence of bradycardia or chronotropic incompetence, permanent pacing should not be performed

section_headings: 5.4.4 Permanent Pacing for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to SND
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that sinus node dysfunction (SND) is diagnosed by combining clinical history and rhythm documentation, with invasive electrophysiology study (EPS) measures such as sinus node recovery time (SNRT) and sinoatrial conduction time (SACT) used only rarely and with limited specificity. Pharmacologic autonomic blockade can aid evaluation, but abnormal SNRT or SACT alone should not justify permanent pacing. The recommendation-specific supportive text notes that EPS is seldom performed solely for sinus node function, may be used adjunctively when noninvasive tests are inconclusive, and carries low but not negligible risk; asymptomatic sinus bradycardia generally does not warrant EPS.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Permanent Pacing for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to SND

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with symptoms that are directly attributable to SND, permanent pacing is indicated to increase heart rate and improve symptoms (S5.4.4-1, S5.4.4-2).

2. In patients who develop symptomatic sinus bradycardia as a consequence of guideline-directed management and therapy for which there is no alternative treatment and continued treatment is clinically necessary, permanent pacing is recommended to increase heart rate and improve symptoms.
3. For patients with tachy-brady syndrome and symptoms attributable to bradycardia, permanent pacing is reasonable to increase heart rate and reduce symptoms attributable to hypoperfusion.
4. In patients with symptomatic chronotropic incompetence, permanent pacing with rate-responsive programming is reasonable to increase exertional heart rates and improve symptoms.

5. In patients with symptoms that are likely attributable to SND, a trial of oral theophylline may be considered to increase heart rate, improve symptoms, and help determine the potential effects of permanent pacing (S5.4.4-3, S5.4.4-4).

content.title: 2018 Bradycardia Guideline
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: Permanent cardiac pacing is indicated to alleviate cerebral hypoperfusion symptoms of bradycardia when reversible causes are excluded. Symptomatic sinus node dysfunction (SND) is the most common indication, followed by atrioventricular block. Pacing benefits quality of life when a clear symptom–bradycardia correlation is established. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: 1) Permanent pacing yields clinical improvement when symptoms correlate directly with sinus bradycardia or pauses, the diagnostic gold standard. 2) Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers can exacerbate SND by reducing sinus node discharge, and pacing allows continuation of essential therapy while managing symptomatic bradycardia. 3) Tachy-brady syndrome involves alternating fast (often AF) and slow rates; severity relates to pause length, but no RCTs have specifically evaluated permanent pacing in this setting. 4) Chronotropic incompetence describes inadequate heart rate response to activity; sensor-based rate-responsive pacing shows mixed benefits, with careful programming required. 5) Theophylline has been studied as an alternative to pacing, showing modest improvement in resting heart rate and symptom burden but inferior symptom control compared with pacing.

section_headings: 5.4.4.1. Permanent Pacing Techniques and Methods for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to SND
content.narrative_summary: The narrative reviews the comparative benefits of atrial-based versus ventricular pacing in symptomatic patients with sinus node dysfunction, highlighting that atrial-based pacing modes reduce atrial fibrillation incidence and preserve atrioventricular synchrony. It summarizes randomized trials showing no mortality difference between dual-chamber and single-chamber atrial pacing but notes additional procedural risks of dual-chamber systems and the potential development of atrioventricular block. The text also discusses pacemaker syndrome, hemodynamic consequences of ventricular dyssynchrony, and when single-chamber ventricular pacing may be reasonable in patients with significant comorbidities or low expected ventricular pacing burden.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Permanent Pacing Techniques and Methods for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to SND

rows.recommendation: In symptomatic patients with SND, atrial-based pacing is recommended over single chamber ventricular pacing (S5.4.4.1-1—S5.4.4.1-4).
In symptomatic patients with SND and intact atrioventricular conduction without evidence of conduction abnormalities, dual chamber or single chamber atrial pacing is recommended (S5.4.4.1-5).

In symptomatic patients with SND who have dual chamber pacemakers and intact atrioventricular conduction, it is reasonable to program the dual chamber pacemaker to minimize ventricular pacing (S5.4.4.1-6).

In symptomatic patients with SND in which frequent ventricular pacing is not expected or the patient has significant comorbidities that are otherwise likely to determine the survival and clinical outcomes, single chamber ventricular pacing is reasonable.

section_headings: 6.1 Pathophysiology, Etiology, and Classification of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews the pathophysiology and etiologies of atrioventricular (AV) block, including congenital and acquired causes such as degenerative, infectious (notably Lyme carditis), ischemic, and iatrogenic factors. AV block is classified anatomically by site—AV nodal, intra-Hisian, and infra-Hisian—with differing prognoses and responses to pacing or vagal influences. The text contrasts first-, second- (Mobitz I and II), and third-degree AV block, describing ECG findings and mechanisms, and emphasizes careful ECG interpretation to avoid misdiagnosis in scenarios like isorhythmic dissociation, junctional rhythms, and atrial bigeminy.

rows.recommendation: For patients with symptomatic SND that is short-lived or infrequent, single chamber ventricular pacing techniques (e.g., current leadless pacing technology) may be adequate for rate support and obviate the requirement for a second pacing lead. Patients with SND who are frail, bedridden, and/or those with limited functional capacity or unfavorable short-term prognosis for survival (<1 year) may not necessarily have a better clinical outcome from strict maintenance of atrioventricular synchrony. Therefore, the benefit afforded by dual chamber pacing may not outweigh the incremental increase in risk. In such patients, a single chamber ventricular pacemaker could provide a more favorable risk-to-benefit profile compared with a dual chamber pacemaker that carries an incremental risk associated with the addition of a second pacing lead.

section_headings: 6.4. Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis reviews nearly 60 years of temporary transvenous pacing, noting early high complication and dislodgement rates that led to limited use, with newer balloon flotation catheters showing improved safety (Figure 5 algorithm). It emphasizes consideration of timing relative to myocardial infarction and primary reperfusion for better outcomes, and describes safety data for prolonged externalized active fixation pacing versus transcutaneous pacing, which is painful and less reliable. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text outlines that semirigid fixed-curve catheters introduced in 1959 had high complication rates, with later balloon-tipped catheters and image-guided venous access reducing risks; prolonged wire placement (>48 hours) delays permanent PPM placement; externalized active-fixation leads (“temporary PPMs”) facilitate longer bridging pacing in antibiotic-treated patients with prior CIED extraction, showing lower dislodgement and complication rates and cost savings; transcutaneous pacing, first reported in 1952 and later combined with defibrillators, has not improved survival in prehospital arrest and is limited by discomfort and unreliable capture, serving mainly as a short-term bridge. Prophylactic pad placement is reasonable in patients at risk of future significant bradycardia. Section 6.4 begins discussion of chronic management with an algorithm in Figure 7.

section_headings: 6.4.1. General Principles of Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block
content.narrative_summary: The presence or absence of symptoms is the primary determinant for permanent pacing in patients with atrioventricular block. Additional considerations include the level of block (nodal versus infranodal), potential deleterious effects of right ventricular pacing, and associated systemic disease that may predispose to progression of block or ventricular arrhythmias. Supportive text outlines scenarios where pacing may not benefit when block is at the AV node without symptom correlation, and when pacing is reserved for significant symptoms or infranodal disease, with monitoring strategies and risk–benefit considerations for device implantation.

content.title: 6.4.2 Transient/Potentially Reversible Causes of Atrioventricular Block
section_headings: 6.4.2 Transient/Potentially Reversible Causes of Atrioventricular Block
content.narrative_summary: Atrioventricular block can result from potentially reversible processes such as metabolic derangements, infections (e.g., Lyme carditis, rheumatic heart disease), medication toxicity (beta-blocker or digoxin overdose), obstructive sleep apnea, or vagal hyperactivity. These blocks often resolve with treatment of the underlying cause—antibiotics, drug withdrawal, or CPAP—though patients remain at risk for recurrent bradycardia. New onset block on chronic nodal blocking therapy may persist despite drug discontinuation, warranting surveillance and possible pacing. Vagally mediated block is usually asymptomatic, with sinus slowing and high-grade block at the AV node. Permanent pacing decisions should balance symptom persistence against procedural risks.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Potentially Reversible or Transient Causes of Atrioventricular Block

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with symptomatic atrioventricular block attributable to a known reversible cause in whom the atrioventricular block does not resolve despite treatment of the underlying cause, permanent pacing is recommended (S6.4.2-1–S6.4.2-3).

2. In patients who had acute atrioventricular block attributable to a known reversible and nonrecurrent cause, and have had complete resolution of the atrioventricular block with treatment of the underlying cause, permanent pacing should not be performed (S6.4.2-1, S6.4.2-4–S6.4.2-9).
3. In patients with asymptomatic vagally mediated atrioventricular block, permanent pacing should not be performed (S6.4.2-6–S6.4.2-10).

section_headings: 6.4.3. Additional Testing for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis emphasizes distinguishing Mobitz type I from type II second-degree atrioventricular block due to differing prognoses and notes that severe first-degree block (PR >0.30 s with narrow QRS) usually indicates nodal delay. Correlating symptoms with rhythm changes via ECG monitoring informs the benefit of permanent pacing. Event monitors and implantable devices (>2 years) provide greater diagnostic yield than 24–48-hour ambulatory ECG. Treadmill exercise testing is useful for exertional symptoms by revealing conduction changes and differentiating infranodal block.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Additional Testing for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block

rows.recommendation: In patients with symptoms (e.g., lightheadedness, dizziness) of unclear etiology who have first-degree atrioventricular block or second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular block on ECG, ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring is reasonable to establish correlation between symptoms and rhythm abnormalities (S6.4.3-1–S6.4.3-4).

In patients with exertional symptoms (e.g., chest pain, shortness of breath) who have first-degree or second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular block at rest, an exercise treadmill test is reasonable to determine whether they may benefit from permanent pacing (S6.4.3-5, S6.4.3-6).

In selected patients with second-degree atrioventricular block, an EPS may be considered to determine the level of the block and to determine whether they may benefit from permanent pacing (S6.4.3-7–S6.4.3-9).

In selected patients with second-degree atrioventricular block, carotid sinus massage and/or pharmacological challenge with atropine, isoproterenol, or procainamide may be considered to determine the level of the block and to determine whether they may benefit from permanent pacing (S6.4.3-10–S6.4.3-12).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Permanent Pacing for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block

rows.recommendation: In patients with acquired second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block, high-grade atrioventricular block, or third-degree atrioventricular block not attributable to reversible or physiologic causes, permanent pacing is recommended regardless of symptoms (S6.4.4-1–S6.4.4-7).

In patients with neuromuscular diseases associated with conduction disorders, including muscular dystrophy (e.g., myotonic dystrophy type 1) or Kearns–Sayre syndrome, who have evidence of second-degree atrioventricular block, third-degree atrioventricular block, or an HV interval of 70 ms or greater, regardless of symptoms, permanent pacing, with additional defibrillator capability if needed and meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected, is recommended (S6.4.4-8–S6.4.4-15).
In patients with permanent AF and symptomatic bradycardia, permanent pacing is recommended (S6.4.4-2, S6.4.4-16, S6.4.4-17).

In patients who develop symptomatic atrioventricular block as a consequence of guideline-directed management and therapy for which there is no alternative treatment and continued treatment is clinically necessary, permanent pacing is recommended to increase heart rate and improve symptoms (S6.4.4-18–S6.4.4-24).

section_headings: 6.4.4.1 Permanent Pacing Techniques and Methods for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block
content.narrative_summary: The page opens mid‐discussion of registry findings on pacemaker dependence and the predictive value of electrocardiographic abnormalities for sudden death in patients with neuromuscular and diabetic conditions, noting limited evidence. After the recommendation table, a synopsis states that recommendations were developed from a systematic review and writing committee review of the literature, including studies on physiologic versus right ventricular pacing in patients with LVEF >35%.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Permanent Pacing Techniques and Methods for Chronic Therapy/Management of Bradycardia Attributable to Atrioventricular Block

rows.recommendation: In patients with SND and atrioventricular block who require permanent pacing, dual chamber pacing is recommended over single chamber ventricular pacing (S6.4.4.1-1–S6.4.4.1-7).

In select patients with atrioventricular block who require permanent pacing in whom frequent ventricular pacing is not expected, or who have significant comorbidities that are likely to determine clinical outcomes and that may limit the benefit of dual chamber pacing, single chamber ventricular pacing is effective (S6.4.4.1-1–S6.4.4.1-6, S6.4.4.1-8–S6.4.4.1-10).

For patients in sinus rhythm with a single chamber ventricular pacemaker who develop pacemaker syndrome, revising to a dual chamber pacemaker is recommended (S6.4.4.1-1, S6.4.4.1-2, S6.4.4.1-5, S6.4.4.1-8–S6.4.4.1-10).

In patients with atrioventricular block who have an indication for permanent pacing with a LVEF between 36% and 50% and are expected to require ventricular pacing more than 40% of the time, it is reasonable to choose pacing methods that maintain physiologic ventricular activation (e.g., cardiac resynchronization therapy [CRT] or His bundle pacing) over right ventricular pacing (S6.4.4.1-7, S6.4.4.1-11–S6.4.4.1-19).

In patients with atrioventricular block who have an indication for permanent pacing with a LVEF between 36% and 50% and are expected to require ventricular pacing less than 40% of the time, it is reasonable to choose right ventricular pacing over pacing methods that maintain physiologic ventricular activation (e.g., CRT or His bundle pacing) (S6.4.4.1-15, S6.4.4.1-16, S6.4.4.1-20, S6.4.4.1-21).

In patients with atrioventricular block at the level of the atrioventricular node who have an indication for permanent pacing, His bundle pacing may be considered to maintain physiologic ventricular activation (S6.4.4.1-19, S6.4.4.1-22–S6.4.4.1-25).
In patients with permanent or persistent AF in whom a rhythm control strategy is not planned, implantation of an atrial lead should not be performed (S6.4.4.1-26, S6.4.4.1-27).

content.title: 7. Conduction Disorders (With 1:1 Atrioventricular Conduction)
content.narrative_summary: This page continues the discussion of QRS abnormalities caused by fascicular and bundle branch blocks within the His-Purkinje system, defines bifascicular block, and distinguishes first-degree atrioventricular block as a conduction disorder rather than an AV block. It summarizes the normal conduction axis, possible developmental, hereditary/genetic, metabolic, infectious, inflammatory, infiltrative, traumatic, ischemic, malignant, or degenerative etiologies of 1:1 atrioventricular conduction disorders, and notes that isolated fascicular and bundle branch blocks may be asymptomatic or signal underlying structural disease. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Evaluation of Conduction Disorders (With 1:1 Atrioventricular Conduction and Normal PR Interval)

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with newly detected LBBB, a transthoracic echocardiogram to exclude structural heart disease is recommended (S7.4-1–S7.4-3).
2. In symptomatic patients with conduction system disease, in whom atrioventricular block is suspected, ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring is useful (S7.4-4–S7.4-11).

3. In selected patients presenting with intraventricular conduction disorders other than LBBB, transthoracic echocardiography is reasonable if structural heart disease is suspected (S7.4-3, S7.4-12, S7.4-13).

4. In patients with symptoms suggestive of intermittent bradycardia (e.g., lightheadedness, syncope), with conduction system disease identified by ECG and no demonstrated atrioventricular block, an EPS is reasonable (S7.4-14).

5. In selected patients with LBBB in whom structural heart disease is suspected and echocardiogram is unrevealing, advanced imaging (e.g., cardiac MRI, computed tomography, or nuclear studies) is reasonable (S7.4-15).

figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Algorithm for evaluation of conduction disorders: start with evidence for conduction disorder, assess for reversible or physiologic causes (e.g., ischemia) and treat if present; if no reversible cause, evaluate for genetic disorder associated with conduction disease; if genetic, proceed to conduction disorders treatment algorithm; if not genetic, assess for suspicions of infiltrative cardiomyopathy, endocarditis, ACHD, etc., and consider advanced imaging (Class IIb) if yes; if no, determine type of conduction disorder (LBBB or RBBB/fascicular block) and perform transthoracic echocardiography (Class I for LBBB, Class IIa for RBBB/fascicular block); treat identified abnormalities; then assess for symptoms suggestive of intermittent bradycardia—if yes, ambulatory ECG monitoring (Class I) and electrophysiology study (Class IIa); if no, ambulatory ECG monitoring (Class IIb) or observe.

section_headings: 7.5. Management of Conduction Disorders (With 1:1 Atrioventricular Conduction)
content.narrative_summary: Continues discussion of progression and implications of left bundle branch block (LBBB), including its low annual progression to high-grade block, associated morbidity, and need for imaging when interpreting ischemic changes. Introduces section 7.5 on the management of conduction disorders with 1:1 atrioventricular conduction and normal PR intervals, emphasizing a patient-centered approach, assessment of underlying disease, baseline ECG patterns, and use of electrophysiology studies to identify infranodal disease. The Synopsis highlights etiologies such as Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy and Kearns-Sayre syndrome, and the predictive value of alternating bundle branch block. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Conduction Disorders (With 1:1 Atrioventricular Conduction and Normal PR Intervals)

rows.recommendation: In patients with syncope and bundle branch block who are found to have an HV interval 70 ms or greater or evidence of infranodal block at EPS, permanent pacing is recommended (S7.5-1, S7.5-2).
In patients with alternating bundle branch block, permanent pacing is recommended (S7.5-3).

In patients with Kearns-Sayre syndrome and conduction disorders, permanent pacing is reasonable, with additional defibrillator capability if appropriate and meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected (S7.5-4, S7.5-5).

In patients with Anderson-Fabry disease and QRS prolongation greater than 110 ms, permanent pacing, with additional defibrillator capability if needed and meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected, may be considered (S7.5-6, S7.5-7).
In patients with heart failure, a mildly to moderately reduced LVEF (36%–50%), and LBBB (QRS ≥150 ms), CRT may be considered (S7.5-8, S7.5-9).
In asymptomatic patients with isolated conduction disease and 1:1 atrioventricular conduction, permanent pacing is not indicated (in the absence of other indications for pacing) (S7.5-10–S7.5-15).

3. In patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery who will likely require future CRT or ventricular pacing, intraoperative placement of a permanent epicardial left ventricular lead may be considered.

section_headings: 8.1.2.3.1. Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement or Repair
content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of postoperative pacing, describing surgical left ventricular lead placement as a stand-alone procedure when coronary sinus placement is unsuccessful, with potential benefits for future atrioventricular nodal ablation and considerations for MRI safety under specialized protocols. It then introduces valvular surgery, noting that the aortic, mitral, and tricuspid valves are most commonly affected, while the pulmonary valve is rarely targeted. Approximately 5% of patients undergoing valve surgery require pacemaker implantation before hospital discharge, with risk factors including preoperative RBBB, multivalve procedures (particularly tricuspid), preoperative LBBB, prolonged PR interval, age >70 years, prior surgery, longer cross-clamp times, and absence of sinus rhythm. Pacing rates vary by valve type: mitral alone 3.5%, aortic alone 5.1%, tricuspid alone 12%, aortic plus mitral 10%, mitral plus tricuspid 16%, and combined aortic, mitral, and tricuspid 25%.

content.narrative_summary: The AV node lies close to the tricuspid valve and is vulnerable during valve repair. Incomplete ring designs help avoid injury. rows.recommendation: 1. In patients undergoing tricuspid valve surgery, routine placement of temporary epicardial pacing wires is recommended (S8.1.2.3.3-1—S8.1.2.3.3-4).

content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis describes that conduction disturbances after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) are common, with new left bundle branch block (LBBB) occurring in 19%–55% of patients and high-degree atrioventricular block in about 10%. Post-TAVR pacing dependency varies and intermittent block may persist. New RBBB increases PPM implantation risk and late mortality; data on LBBB’s impact on outcomes are mixed, though early PPM for LBBB does not mitigate increased mortality.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Bradycardia in Adults With Adult Congenital Heart Disease

rows.recommendation: In adults with adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) and symptomatic SND or chronotropic incompetence, atrial based permanent pacing is recommended (S8.2-1—S8.2-6).
In adults with ACHD and symptomatic bradycardia related to atrioventricular block, permanent pacing is recommended (S8.2-7—S8.2-9).

In adults with congenital complete atrioventricular block with any symptomatic bradycardia, a wide QRS escape rhythm, mean daytime heart rate below 50 bpm, complex ventricular ectopy, or ventricular dysfunction, permanent pacing is recommended (S8.2-10, S8.2-11).

In adults with ACHD and postoperative second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block, high-grade atrioventricular block, or third-degree atrioventricular block that is not expected to resolve, permanent pacing is recommended (S8.2-12, S8.2-13).
In asymptomatic adults with congenital complete atrioventricular block, permanent pacing is reasonable (S8.2-7—S8.2-11).
In adults with repaired ACHD who require permanent pacing for bradycardia indications, a bradycardia device with atrial antitachycardia pacing capabilities is reasonable (S8.2-14, S8.2-15).

In adults with ACHD with preexisting sinus node and/or atrioventricular conduction disease who are undergoing cardiac surgery, intraoperative placement of epicardial permanent pacing leads is reasonable.
In adults with ACHD and pacemakers, atrial-based permanent pacing for the prevention of atrial arrhythmias may be considered (S8.2-3—S8.2-5, S8.2-16).
In selected adults with ACHD and venous to systemic intracardiac shunts, placement of endocardial pacing leads is potentially harmful (S8.2-17, S8.2-18).

section_headings: 8.3. Management of Bradycardia in Patients With an Acute MI
content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion on atrial arrhythmias in congenital heart disease (bullets 8–9), noting 40–45% incidence, mixed trial results of atrial-based versus ventricular pacing, and lead thrombus/vegetations despite anticoagulation, with individualized nonconventional pacing strategies. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Bradycardia in the Context of Acute MI

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients presenting with an acute MI, temporary pacing is indicated for medically refractory symptomatic or hemodynamically significant bradycardia related to SND or atrioventricular block (S8.3-1–S8.3-4).
2. Patients who present with SND or atrioventricular block in the setting of an acute MI should undergo a waiting period before determining the need for permanent pacing (S8.3-1, S8.3-4–S8.3-7).

3. In patients presenting with an acute MI with second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block, high-grade atrioventricular block, alternating bundle-branch block, or third-degree atrioventricular block (persistent or infranodal), permanent pacing is indicated after a waiting period (S8.3-7, S8.3-8).

4. In patients with an acute MI with symptomatic or hemodynamically significant sinus bradycardia or atrioventricular block at the level of the atrioventricular node, the administration of atropine is reasonable (S8.3-9–S8.3-11).
5. In patients with an acute MI and transient atrioventricular block that resolves, permanent pacing should not be performed (S8.3-1, S8.3-4, S8.3-7, S8.3-12–S8.3-16).

6. In patients with an acute MI and a new bundle-branch block or isolated fascicular block in the absence of second-degree or third-degree atrioventricular block, permanent pacing should not be performed (S8.3-17–S8.3-19).
